She reports that her son has been arrested multiple times and can often be aggressive getting into fights. As a teenager, he would lie to obtain money, played truant and would say unpleasant hurtful things to her without apology or apparent regret. He has never held down a job and relies on his parents for financial support. His mother has the name of the condition he has been diagnosed with and knows you are not able to discuss the individual case. She asks if you can provide generic information on his condition to aid her understanding as she has always blamed herself for his behaviour. What is the most likely condition her son has been diagnosed with?
explanation:
Antisocial personality disorder
Patients with antisocial personality disorder often fail to conform to social norms, and show lack of remorse, deception and irresponsibility. The correct answer here is 2 - antisocial personality disorder. Patients with this condition often fail to comply with social norms in terms of lawful behaviour resulting in multiple arrests. They are prone to getting into fights due to aggressiveness and can be deceitful particularly when seeking material gain. They can have a disregard for the safety of themselves and others and are irresponsible, failing to support themselves financially. When they do act inappropriately or in a hurtful way to others, they are unable to show remorse for their actions. There is often a history of problems such as truancy in childhood. Their behaviour can have a significant impact on family life and so it is understandable that his mother may have blamed herself in the past and want more information. It is important to ensure that during this consultation confidentiality is not breached.

Avoidant personality disorder
Patients with avoidant personality disorder tend to avoid social contact/relationships due to fear of being criticised, rejected or embarrassed. They view themselves as inferior to others and so are not keen to be involved unless they are certain of being liked. Hence this is not the correct answer.

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is characterised by emotional instability, impulsive behaviour and intense but unstable relationships with others. Patients often have feelings of emptiness, poor self-image and recurrent attempts at self-harm. Again making this an incorrect answer.

Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder is also incorrect. These patients have an over exaggerated perception of self-importance, lack empathy and tend to have a sense of entitlement.

Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic personality disorder is seen in patients who crave to be the centre of attention. They can also be sexually inappropriate and suggestible and as such, this is not the correct answer.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted following a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She has a history of alcohol dependence and was last seen drinking 48 hours ago. On examination, she is tremulous and agitated with a heart rate of 110 bpm and blood pressure 165/95 mmHg. Blood tests show no significant abnormalities. She is commenced on chlordiazepoxide as part of an alcohol withdrawal protocol. Which mechanism best explains the therapeutic action of this medication?
options: Increases duration of chloride channel opening
Increases frequency of chloride channel opening
explanation:
Increases frequency of chloride channel opening
Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) by increasing the frequency of chloride channels. Increases frequency of chloride channel opening is the correct answer. Benzodiazepines, including chlordiazepoxide, work by enhancing the effect of GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. They bind to GABAA receptors and increase the frequency with which chloride channels open in response to GABA binding. This leads to increased chloride influx, hyperpolarisation of neurons, and reduced neuronal excitability. This mechanism makes benzodiazepines effective in managing alcohol withdrawal syndrome, which results from sudden cessation of alcohol's GABAergic effects. The anticonvulsant, anxiolytic, and sedative properties of chlordiazepoxide are all mediated through this enhanced GABAergic inhibition.

Increases duration of chloride channel opening
Increases duration of chloride channel opening describes the mechanism of barbiturates, not benzodiazepines. While both drug classes enhance GABAergic transmission through GABAA receptors, barbiturates prolong the time that chloride channels remain open rather than increasing the frequency of opening. This distinction is clinically important as barbiturates have a narrower therapeutic index and greater risk of respiratory depression.

Blocks glutamate receptors
Blocks glutamate receptors is not the mechanism of benzodiazepines. Glutamate receptor antagonists, such as memantine (which blocks NMDA receptors), work through a different pathway. While alcohol does have some NMDA antagonist effects, benzodiazepines do not share this mechanism.

Enhances serotonin reuptake
Enhances serotonin reuptake is incorrect and would actually reduce serotonergic transmission. Benzodiazepines do not significantly affect serotonin pathways. This option describes the opposite effect to SSRIs, which inhibit serotonin reuptake.

Inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels
Inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels is the mechanism of action of certain anticonvulsants such as gabapentin and pregabalin, as well as some antihypertensive medications. This is not how benzodiazepines exert their therapeutic effects in alcohol withdrawal or seizure management.

stem: A 54-year-old man is brought to his general practitioner by his wife. She is concerned that he is not eating or drinking. He has a past medical history of depression. Upon further questioning from his general practitioner, the patient reports that he sees no point in eating because he believes himself to be non-existent. What is the correct description of what he is experiencing?
explanation:
Cotard syndrome
Cotard syndrome is characterised by a person believing they are dead or non-existent. This is nihilistic delusional ideation whereby a patient believes they are dead or non-existent. It is associated with depression.

Capgras syndrome
Capgras syndrome. This is a delusional disorder whereby a patient believes that someone close to them has been replaced by an imposter.

Couvade syndrome
Couvade syndrome is incorrect. This is also known as a 'sympathetic pregnancy' is a disorder whereby biological fathers suffer the symptoms of pregnancy in the 1st and 3rd trimesters.

De Clerambault's syndrome
De Clerambault's Syndrome is incorrect. This is a delusional disorder whereby the patient thinks another person (typically wealthy or famous) is in love with them.

Fregoli delusion
Fregoli delusion is incorrect. This is a delusional disorder whereby the patient believes that different people are in fact the same person in disguise.

stem: The sister of a 34-year-old man comes to see you in clinic as she is worried her brother may have a personality disorder. She reports her brother has always had a heightened opinion of himself and often expresses delusional thoughts regarding his potential for success as a banker believing he is capable of making millions. He does not seem perturbed by bringing others down in the process and appears pleased when he talks of others failures. She remembers he behaved similarly when they were growing up and was unsympathetic towards her when she had to resit her finals due to ill health. What personality disorder is she describing?
explanation:
Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personalities lack empathy, have a sense of entitlement, and take advantage of others to achieve their own needs. The correct answer is narcissistic personality disorder. Whilst her brother may not actually qualify for having a personality disorder if his behaviour does not cause him personal distress or prevent him functioning socially, many of these features are seen in narcissistic behaviour. These patients have a heightened impression of self-importance and entitlement, often believing they have unlimited abilities to succeed, become powerful, or look beautiful. Additionally, they lack empathy and will happily take advantage of others to achieve their own needs. In keeping with many personality disorders, his symptoms appear to have been present since childhood and into adult life.

Antisocial personality disorder
Patients with antisocial personality disorder also lack empathy or feelings of guilt/remorse. Similarly to narcissistic personalities, they can be deceitful when wanting to achieve their own needs. However, in contrast to narcissists, they often fail to comply with rules or laws, resulting in criminal offences and are prone to getting into fights. As such, the patient in the stem fits more closely with narcissistic personality disorder.

Schizoid personality disorder
Patients with schizoid personality disorder tend to have a lack of interest in sexual interactions, are cold, and lack close friendships, preferring to spend time alone. They are also indifferent to praise, making this unlikely to be the correct answer.

Schizotypal personality disorder
Patients with schizotypal personality disorder can have odd/eccentric beliefs or behavior. They can also struggle to make friends and can be paranoid/suspicious as opposed to lacking empathy or having a sense of entitlement.

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is characterized by emotional instability, impulsive behavior, feelings of emptiness, and recurrent attempts at self-harm.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a two-week history of weakness in her left leg and sensory loss in her right arm. She has no past medical history. She is a professional rower who has recently been disappointed by not being selected for the Olympic team. On examination, she walks without apparent difficulty, but testing reveals 0/5 strength during hip extension in the left leg. Involuntary extension of the left hip occurs when she is asked to flex the right hip. Reflexes are normal and there is decreased sensation in the right upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder is the correct diagnosis. This condition commonly presents with a loss of motor and sensory function, which typically arises during periods of stress. For a professional rower, not qualifying for the Olympic games would likely be an immensely stressful event. Hoover's sign is a clinical test used to evaluate functional neurological disorders, assessing for discrepancies between voluntary and involuntary hip extension. In cases of genuine limb paresis, both voluntary and involuntary hip extension would be rated as 0/5 in strength. To perform the test, voluntary hip extension is initially assessed in the 'weak' limb. Should this reveal weakness, the examiner subsequently tests hip flexion in the contralateral limb while placing their hand beneath the heel of the patient's 'weak' limb. Ordinarily, hip flexion on one side results in automatic contralateral hip extension. Absence of this response may indicate true weakness; however, if involuntary hip extension is observed, it suggests an inconsistency between voluntary and involuntary movements, raising suspicion for a functional neurological disorder. Functional weakness is characteristic of conversion disorders; importantly, there is no indication that this patient is simulating weakness for secondary gain.

Hypochondriasis
Hypochondriasis is not applicable here. Hypochondriasis involves a preoccupation with having a serious illness based on misinterpretation of bodily symptoms rather than fear associated with a specific diagnosis such as cancer alone. The patient does not exhibit concern over any particular diagnosis; thus, this option does not apply.

Malingering
Malingering is also incorrect for this scenario. Malingering involves fabricating or exaggerating symptoms to obtain external benefits or rewards. In this case study, there are no discernible advantages that could motivate the patient to feign neurological symptoms; rather, it appears more consistent with stress-induced conversion disorder.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder does not fit the clinical picture either. This psychiatric condition involves multiple unexplained physical complaints persisting for more than two years without identifiable medical explanations. As somatisation pertains to subjective symptoms reported by patients rather than objective signs detected by clinicians during examination, this diagnosis does not align with our findings.

Stroke
Finally, stroke can be ruled out due to an absence of characteristic stroke-related patterns of weakness—namely unilateral distribution—and because strokes typically do not present with inconsistent examination findings like those described here (e.g., ambulating into the emergency department but demonstrating provoked weakness). Therefore, stroke is deemed an unlikely diagnosis in this context.

stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought for review. He is normally fit and well and hasn't seen a doctor for over five years. His mother has been increasingly concerned about his behaviour in the past few weeks. She describes him staying up late at night, talking quickly and being very irritable. Yesterday he told his mother he was planning to 'take-over' the school assembly and give 'constructive criticism' to his teachers in front of the other pupils. He feels many of his teachers are 'underperforming' and need to be 'retaught' their subjects by him. He admits to trying cannabis once around six months ago and has drank alcohol 'a few times' in the past year, the last time being two weeks ago. Prior to his deterioration a few weeks ago his mother describes him as a happy, well-adjusted, sociable young man. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mania
The delusions of grandeur imply this is mania rather than hypomania.

Hypomania
The delusions of grandeur imply this is mania rather than hypomania.

Cannabis-induced psychosis
Cannabis and alcohol related problems are very unlikely given how long ago he used those substances.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with known rheumatoid arthritis, established on sulfasalazine as well as regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, is reviewed by her GP with ongoing low mood. Non-pharmacological interventions have been trialled with limited improvement, and the patient now reports worsening depressive symptoms. The GP decides to commence the patient on an antidepressant. Which agent would increase this patient’s risk of gastrointestinal bleeding the most, and therefore warrant proton pump inhibitor cover?
explanation:
Citalopram
Citalopram is a common selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRIs), which are now considered the first-line treatment for most patients with depression. As the name suggests SSRIs increase the extracellular level of serotonin by limiting its reabsorption at the pre-synapses. Gastrointestinal (GI) disruption is common with SSRI use, and they are associated with a significant risk of GI bleeding. It is thought SSRI potential deplete platelet serotonin, resulting in a reduction in clot formation, therefore, increasing the risk of bleeding. As this patient is already established on an NSAID the addition of an SSRI will increase her risk of GI bleeding further and therefore a protein pump inhibitor (PPI) should also be prescribed.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) that can be used in the management of major depressive disorders as well as several different pain syndromes. Amitriptyline inhibits serotonin transporter (SERT) and norepinephrine transporter (NET) both increasing neurotransmitter availability. The main adverse effects of TCAs are related to their anticholinergic effects resulting in symptoms such as blurred vision, dry mouth, and constipation etc. GI bleeds are not commonly associated with TCAs.

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic, rarely used for patients with severe depression and psychotic symptoms. It blocks receptors in the brain's dopamine pathways and therefore the main adverse effects include, extrapyramidal side effects (akathisia, dystonia etc), hypotension and anticholinergic effects. Again GI bleeds are rare.

Selegiline
Selegiline is a selective and irreversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B), and therefore in the class of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). MAOIs are used as antidepressants and work by preventing the breakdown of monoamine neurotransmitters, increasing their availability. MAOIs have been associated with an increased risk of serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crises but GI bleeds are rare.

St John's Wort
Hypericum perforatum, commonly known as St John's Wort is a plant frequently used in alternative medicine, particularly for the management of depression. Although its use remains controversial multiple studies have indicated it may have superiority over placebo on treating mild to moderate depression, with the active ingredients thought to be hypericin and hyperforin. St John's wort can interfere with other medications, and its use with other antidepressants is associated with an increased risk of serotonin syndrome, however, it has not been associated with an increased risk of GI bleeding.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to her GP with troubling symptoms. Eight weeks ago, she was involved in a severe road traffic accident. Although physically well after the accident, she reports experiencing flashbacks since then, being overly vigilant when crossing the road, and generally having difficulty focusing at work. Which of the following features would best support the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Emotional detachment
The correct answer is emotional detachment. The diagnosis here is that of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), with these symptoms being present for over 1 month following a traumatic experience. Patients are often emotionally numbed - demonstrating an inability to experience feelings fully, and generally feeling detached emotionally.

Delusional beliefs
Delusional beliefs do not usually manifest in PTSD. If she were displaying signs of this, it would be prudent to consider an alternative diagnosis, as this is a psychotic feature.

Excessive sleep
Excessive sleep is not usually part of PTSD - the opposite is normally true. Patients have difficulty sleeping, often wake up during the night, and experience nightmares.

Nystagmus
Nystagmus is not associated with PTSD. There is, however, a link between eyes and PTSD - the current conventional therapy for PTSD is eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy.

Paranoid ideation
Paranoid ideation is also not usually a feature of PTSD. If this were being displayed, alternative diagnoses should be considered.

stem: A 72-year-old man who is having trouble sleeping is prescribed temazepam. What is the mechanism of action of temazepam?
options: Enhances the effect of gamma-aminobutyric acid
explanation:
Enhances the effect of gamma-aminobutyric acid
Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) by increasing the frequency of chloride channels. The correct answer is Enhances the effect of gamma-aminobutyric acid. Temazepam belongs to a class of drugs known as benzodiazepines. Its mechanism of action involves enhancing the effect of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. This enhancement is achieved by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening within the GABA-A receptor complex, leading to hyperpolarisation of neurons and ultimately decreased neuronal excitability.

Inhibits the effect of acetylcholine
Inhibits the effect of acetylcholine is not correct. Anticholinergic drugs inhibit the effects of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter involved in many functions including muscle movement, heart rate regulation, learning and memory. Examples include atropine and scopolamine. Temazepam does not have this mechanism.

Inhibits the effect gamma-aminobutyric acid
Inhibits the effect gamma-aminobutyric acid is also incorrect. Drugs that inhibit GABA usually increase neuronal activity rather than decrease it, which can lead to seizures or anxiety rather than sedation. An example would be flumazenil, a GABA antagonist used as an antidote for benzodiazepine overdose.

Inhibits the effect of glutamate
Inhibits the effect of glutamate is not correct either. Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter in CNS and its inhibition would indeed result in reduced neuronal activity similar to enhancing GABA's effects. However, temazepam doesn't work by inhibiting glutamate; drugs that do this are typically NMDA receptor antagonists like memantine used in Alzheimer's disease treatment.

Inhibits the effect of noradrenaline
Inhibits the effect of noradrenaline is also incorrect. Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) inhibitors are typically used as antihypertensives or antidepressants such as beta-blockers or selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (NARIs). They do not primarily induce sleep or reduce anxiety which are key therapeutic effects of temazepam.

stem: A 61-year-old businessman presents with a 3-year history of severe itchiness and sores containing 'white fibres' which he said are living 'bugs'. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medication. On examination, there are well-demarcated, scooped-out clean ulcerations with occasional white filaments, some hypopigmented patches, and extensive chronic excoriations. There is sparring between the scapula. Multiple and extensive dermatology and infectious disease outpatient investigations and treatments have failed to find a cause nor improve symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Delusional parasitosis
Patient with a fixed, false belief (delusion) that they are infested by 'bugs' → delusional parasitosis. Delusional parasitosis is the correct answer, as this patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with 'Morgellons' which is regarded as a form of delusional parasitosis. Reported fibres or inanimate materials are often found to be common household/clothing materials (e.g. cotton). Skin lesions are consistent with chronic excoriations and the scooped-out lesion is consistent with repetitive picking of lesions. The hypopigmented patches are healed lesions. Sparring of the area between the scapula indicates the area the hands are unable to reach, and no lesions were evident there.

Body dysmorphic disorder
Body dysmorphic disorder is a persistent preoccupation of one or more aspects of one's own physical appearance, in a derogatory manner. The aspect in question is either normal or has only minor defects.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder manifests as neurological symptoms (e.g. weakness, non-epileptic seizures, negative sensory symptoms, movement disorders) without any identifiable structural pathology.

Somatic symptom disorder
Somatic symptom disorder is a mental disorder characterised by physical symptoms (e.g. pain, weakness, shortness of breath) of which there is no objective evidence of pathology, AND is associated with the excessive preoccupation of these symptoms.

Tactile hallucinations
Tactile hallucinations is not a diagnosis; however, it is a symptom present in patients with delusional parasitosis. The question was asking for a diagnosis.

stem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the doctors by his daughter. Four weeks ago his wife died from metastatic breast cancer. He reports being tearful every day but his daughter is concerned because he is constantly 'picking fights' with her over minor matters and issues relating to their family past. The daughter also reports that he has on occasion described hearing his wife talking to him and on one occasion he prepared a meal for her. Despite this he has started going walking again with friends and says that he is determined to get 'back on track'. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Normal grief reaction
The correct answer is Normal grief reaction. This patient is displaying typical features of normal grief following bereavement. The symptoms described - tearfulness, irritability, and even transient hallucinations of the deceased (hearing wife's voice) - are common and normal experiences during the acute grief period. Importantly, the patient maintains some positive functioning by continuing social activities (walking with friends) and shows motivation to improve ('get back on track'), indicating this is not pathological. The maintained functioning and relatively short timeframe support this being a normal grief process.

Atypical grief reaction
Atypical grief reaction would typically involve more severe symptoms that persist beyond 6-12 months, with significant functional impairment. The timeframe here (4 weeks) and maintained functioning suggests this is not atypical.

Depression without psychotic features
Depression without psychotic features would typically present with more pervasive symptoms including loss of interest/pleasure, significant sleep/appetite changes, and more profound functional impairment. The patient's maintained social activities and future-oriented thinking make this less likely.

Delusional disorder
Delusional disorder is incorrect as the brief sensory experiences described are common in acute grief and do not represent true delusions. The patient appears to maintain insight and reality testing.

Depression with psychotic features
Depression with psychotic features would involve more severe depressive symptoms along with fixed false beliefs or persistent hallucinations. The transient nature of the sensory experiences and maintained functioning make this diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 23-year-old man asks to be referred to a plastic surgeon. From his records you can see he has been treated for anxiety and depression with fluoxetine previously and has been off work with back pain for the past three months. He is concerned that his ears are too big in proportion to his face. He reports that he now seldom leaves the house because of this. On examination his ears appear to be within normal limits. What is the most appropriate description of this behaviour?
explanation:
Dysmorphophobia
The correct answer in this scenario is Dysmorphophobia. Dysmorphophobia, also known as body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), is a mental health condition where an individual obsesses over perceived flaws or defects in their appearance that are either minor or not observable by others. In this case, the patient believes his ears are too big in proportion to his face, despite them appearing within normal limits upon examination. This preoccupation with his appearance has led him to avoid social situations and become housebound.

Hypochondriasis
Hypochondriasis, now referred to as illness anxiety disorder, is a condition where a person becomes excessively worried about having a serious illness based on normal bodily sensations or minor symptoms. The focus here is on the fear of having an illness rather than concerns about physical appearance.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterized by excessive and persistent worry about various aspects of life, such as work, health, family, and finances. Although it may be possible for someone with GAD to worry about their appearance as well, the primary concern in this case appears to be specifically related to the size of the patient's ears rather than generalized anxiety.

Somatisation
Somatisation refers to the process by which psychological distress manifests itself through physical symptoms. In this scenario, there are no physical symptoms reported by the patient - his distress relates solely to his perception of his ears' size.

Malingering
Malingering involves intentionally feigning or exaggerating physical or psychological symptoms for personal gain, such as financial compensation or avoiding work responsibilities. In this case, there is no evidence suggesting that the patient's concerns about his ears are fabricated for personal gain.

stem: You are considering prescribing a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for a patient with depression. Which class of drug is most likely to interact with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor?
explanation:
Triptan
Triptans should be avoided in patients taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor due to the increased risk of serotonin syndrome.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents as he is concerned about a number of recent episodes related to sleep. He finds when he wakes up and less often when he is falling asleep he is 'paralysed' and unable to move. This sometimes associated with what the patient describes as 'hallucinations' such as seeing another person in the room. He is becoming increasingly anxious about these recent episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sleep paralysis
The correct answer is sleep paralysis. Sleep paralysis is a condition characterized by the inability to move or speak when transitioning between sleep and wakefulness, either when falling asleep or upon awakening. It can be accompanied by vivid hallucinations, which may explain the patient's description of seeing another person in the room. Sleep paralysis is generally harmless but can cause significant anxiety for those who experience it.

Frontal lobe epilepsy
Frontal lobe epilepsy is a type of focal epilepsy that originates in the frontal lobes of the brain. While seizures in frontal lobe epilepsy can occur during sleep and present with unusual behaviours or movements, they would not typically cause the sensation of paralysis described by the patient.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterized by excessive and persistent worry about various aspects of life, which might include concerns about one's health. However, GAD does not directly cause episodes of sleep-related paralysis or hallucinations.

Night terrors
Night terrors are episodes of intense fear and agitation that occur during deep non-REM sleep. They are more common in children but can also affect adults. During a night terror episode, an individual may scream, thrash around, or exhibit other signs of distress; however, they do not experience paralysis as described by the patient.

Acute schizophrenia
Acute schizophrenia is a chronic mental health disorder characterized by symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behaviour, and negative symptoms like diminished emotional expression. While hallucinations may be present in schizophrenia patients, the specific pattern of sleep-related paralysis described by this patient does not align with typical manifestations of acute schizophrenia.

stem: A 73-year-old male patient who lives alone presents with recurrent episodes of pleasant visual hallucinations but no clouding of consciousness or confusion. He tells you he knows the hallucinations are not real. He is normally fit and well with the exception of visual impairment. Given the likely diagnosis, what ophthalmic condition is he most likely to suffer from?
explanation:
Age-related macular degeneration
Age-related macular degeneration is associated with Charles-Bonnet syndrome. This patient has Charles-Bonnet syndrome (CBS) as evidenced by visual hallucinations with normal insight on a background of visual impairment. He also lives alone which could be another risk factor for CBS if this leads to him becoming socially isolated. 11-15% of patients with severe visual impairment are thought to have coexisting CBS and experience recurrent, persistent or episodic visual or auditory hallucinations. The most common ophthalmological condition associated with CBS is age-related macular degeneration and hence this is the correct answer.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma and cataract are the next most common causes of visual impairment associated with CBS. However, they are less common than age-related macular degeneration.

Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy is a less common cause of visual impairment associated with CBS compared to age-related macular degeneration.

Retinal detachment
Retinal detachment is a less common cause of visual impairment associated with CBS compared to age-related macular degeneration.

Cataract
Glaucoma and cataract are the next most common causes of visual impairment associated with CBS. However, they are less common than age-related macular degeneration.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of hallucinations. He describes often seeing faces smaller than normal or other objects out of proportion. He finds these episodes distressing although he says he knows they're not real. His past medical history includes macular degeneration and an episode of depression 20 years ago following the death of his wife. Neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Charles-Bonnet syndrome
The most likely diagnosis in this case is Charles-Bonnet syndrome. This condition is characterized by complex visual hallucinations in individuals with visual impairment, such as macular degeneration, which the patient has. The hallucinations are often of faces or objects that are smaller or larger than normal. Importantly, patients with Charles-Bonnet syndrome maintain insight into the unreal nature of their hallucinations and do not have other cognitive or psychiatric symptoms.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is an unlikely diagnosis in this case because the patient's age and presentation do not fit the typical pattern for schizophrenia. Schizophrenia usually presents earlier in life and involves a range of positive and negative symptoms beyond just hallucinations, such as delusions, disorganized thinking, and social withdrawal.

Psychotic depression
Psychotic depression can present with hallucinations; however, these are more commonly auditory rather than visual. Additionally, there is no indication in the patient's history that he is currently experiencing depressive symptoms. His previous episode of depression occurred 20 years ago following a significant life event (the death of his wife) and does not necessarily suggest a current depressive episode.

Cerebral tumour
A cerebral tumour could potentially cause hallucinations; however, it would be less likely to cause recurrent episodes without any other accompanying neurological signs or symptoms. The patient's neurological examination was unremarkable, making this diagnosis less probable.

Alzheimer's disease
Alzheimer's disease is also an unlikely diagnosis given the patient's isolated symptomatology. While Alzheimer's disease can present with various neuropsychiatric symptoms including hallucinations, it would typically involve progressive cognitive decline and memory impairment as well. There is no mention of such features in this case.

stem: A 77-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath, productive cough and confusion. She is treated for delirium, secondary to a chest infection, with intravenous antibiotics and admitted to the geriatrics ward for observation. Overnight, she becomes agitated and restless. Initial measures to settle her are unsuccessful; the on-call doctor prescribes haloperidol, which takes effect quickly and reduces her agitation. What receptor does this drug primarily antagonise?
explanation:
D2
Haloperidol is a first-generation, 'typical' antipsychotic commonly used for a number of purposes. Apart from its use as an antipsychotic in psychiatric patients, it is often used in the context of delirium as seen here. It also plays a role in the management of nausea, especially in the palliative setting. It binds to numerous receptors, with different affinities for each. Primarily, it antagonises the dopamine D2 receptor. Haloperidol also antagonises the serotonin 5HT2 receptor. However, its effect on the D2 receptor is far more effective at any given concentration.

5HT2
Haloperidol also antagonises the serotonin 5HT2 receptor. However, its effect on the D2 receptor is far more effective at any given concentration.

5HT3
The drug is not known to significantly affect the serotonin 5HT3 receptor. Examples of antagonists of this receptor include the antiemetic ondansetron and newer-generation, 'atypical' antipsychotics such as quetiapine and olanzapine.

D1
The drug also binds to the dopamine D1 receptor. However, this effect is not as significant as the effect on the D2 receptor.

H1
Haloperidol has some effect on the histamine H1 receptor. This effect, however, requires much higher concentrations of haloperidol.

stem: A 38-year-old man is reviewed by his general practitioner. He reports difficulties in maintaining positive relationships with colleagues. On further questioning, it becomes clear that the man has a very strict value system and moral code. He is inflexible with respect to different beliefs and work practices and this inflexibility makes it difficult to form relationships with colleagues, collaborate or delegate. What type of personality disorder best describes this patient?
explanation:
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Patients with obsessive-compulsive personality can be rigid with respect to morals, ethics and values and often are reluctant to surrender work to others. An obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is correct. Patients with this personality disorder are very rigid with respect to morals, ethics and values and are reluctant to surrender work to others, as in this case. Other features are preoccupation with details, rules, lists and orders and perfectionism impairing the ability to complete tasks.

Antisocial personality disorder
An antisocial personality disorder is incorrect. This personality disorder is characterized by aggression, repeated unlawful behaviour, deception and aggression.

Borderline personality disorder
A borderline personality disorder is incorrect. This personality disorder is characterized by an unstable self-image, unstable interpersonal relationships, efforts to avoid abandonment and chronic feelings of emptiness.

Narcissistic personality disorder
The narcissistic personality is incorrect. This is characterized by a grandiose sense of self-importance, sense of entitlement, lack of empathy and preoccupation with fantasies of unlimited success, power or beauty.

Paranoid personality disorder
A paranoid personality disorder is incorrect. This personality disorder is characterized by hypersensitivity to insult, an unwarranted tendency to question the loyalty of friends and preoccupation with conspiratorial beliefs and hidden meaning.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presents with nausea, headaches and palpitations. He has had multiple previous admissions with such symptoms over the past 2 years, each time no organic cause was found. What kind of disorder is this likely to represent?
explanation:
Somatisation disorder
This condition is characterised by the recurrent presentation of physical symptoms such as nausea, headaches, and palpitations in the absence of a detectable organic cause. These symptoms are not intentionally produced or feigned, distinguishing it from factitious disorders like Munchausen's syndrome. The patient may have multiple admissions over years due to these unexplained symptoms, which can cause significant distress and impairment in their daily life.

Munchausen's syndrome
Munchausen's syndrome, also known as factitious disorder imposed on self, involves individuals deliberately producing or feigning physical or psychological symptoms. They do this to assume the sick role and gain attention or sympathy. However, there is no indication in the question that the patient is intentionally causing his own symptoms.

Hypochondrial disorder
Hypochondrial disorder, now referred to as Illness Anxiety Disorder in DSM-5, involves a preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness. Patients with this condition misinterpret normal bodily sensations as signs of serious illness. However, they usually do not experience actual somatic symptoms like those described in the question.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder, also known as Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (FNSD), typically presents with neurological symptoms such as paralysis, blindness, or seizures that cannot be explained by medical evaluation. The presented case does not describe any such neurological symptom.

Dissociative disorder
Dissociative disorder involves disruptions or gaps in memory, awareness, identity or perception that are too extreme to be considered mere forgetfulness. These disorders often develop as a way to cope with trauma. The lack of any indications of such disruptions makes this option unlikely for the given case scenario.

stem: Which one of the following interventions is most likely to be beneficial in a patient with schizophrenia?
explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy
The correct answer is Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, CBT is recommended for all people with schizophrenia. This form of therapy helps patients deal with their symptoms by changing the way they think and behave. It can reduce the severity of symptoms and improve quality of life. In conclusion, while all these interventions may play a role in managing different aspects of schizophrenia according to individual needs and circumstances, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy stands out as being most likely beneficial due to its comprehensive approach towards symptom management according to NICE guidelines.

Counselling
The first incorrect option, Counselling, while beneficial in many mental health conditions, has not been proven as the most effective intervention in schizophrenia. Counselling typically involves talking about feelings and emotions related to personal experiences, but it does not specifically target the cognitive distortions or delusional beliefs common in schizophrenia.

Supportive psychotherapy
Supportive psychotherapy is another incorrect option. This type of therapy aims to foster a therapeutic relationship between patient and therapist to enhance self-esteem, reduce anxiety, and improve adaptive skills. However, it doesn't directly address the cognitive distortions that are characteristic of schizophrenia.

Social skills training
Social skills training, although useful in improving social functioning in individuals with schizophrenia, is not considered as effective as CBT in managing the overall symptoms of the disease. Social skills training focuses on teaching patients how to interact more effectively with others, which can be beneficial but does not directly target psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions.

Adherence therapy
Adherence therapy is also an incorrect choice. Adherence therapy aims at improving medication compliance through education about illness and treatment benefits. While this may be helpful for some patients who struggle with medication adherence, it doesn't address cognitive distortions or other core symptoms of schizophrenia like CBT does.

stem: Which of the following types of tricyclic antidepressant is considered the safest in overdosage?
explanation:
Lofepramine
Lofepramine is a third-generation tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) and is considered the safest in overdosage due to its lower cardiotoxicity compared with other TCAs. This reduced cardiotoxicity is because lofepramine has less affinity for cardiac fast sodium channels, which are responsible for the life-threatening arrhythmias associated with TCA overdose.

Nortriptyline
Nortriptyline is a second-generation TCA and while it has a lower risk of cardiotoxicity compared to first-generation TCAs, it still presents a significant risk in overdose situations. Its side effects can include tachycardia, QT interval prolongation, and complete heart block.

Imipramine
Imipramine, another second-generation TCA, also carries a higher risk of cardiotoxicity in overdose than lofepramine. It may cause serious cardiovascular complications such as arrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, and even cardiac arrest.

Dosulepin
Dosulepin (also known as Dothiepin) has been shown to have the highest fatality rate in overdose of all TCAs according to UK data from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths. It can lead to severe cardiovascular toxicity including tachycardia, hypotension, and QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes.

Clomipramine
Clomipramine is another second-generation TCA that carries significant risk in overdosage. It can cause seizures at relatively low levels of overdose and has strong anticholinergic effects which can lead to dangerous conditions like paralytic ileus.

stem: A 20-year-old student drinks around 500 ml of vodka at a party. The next morning he feels thirsty and finds he is passing more urine than normal. Which one of the following best explains why people who drink excessive amounts alcohol develop polyuria?
options: Ethanol induces vasoconstriction of the renal arteries
Ethanol increases aquaporin proteins in the proximal convoluted tubule
Supratentorial reflex to cleanse the body of toxins
explanation:
Ethanol inhibits ADH secretion
Ethanol reduces the calcium-dependent secretion of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) by blocking channels in the neurohypophyseal nerve terminal.

stem: Carol is a 57-year-old lady who is under a section 3 at a an inpatient psychiatric hospital. She has stopped eating or drinking as she believes she is dead and does not require food anymore. Which syndrome is characterised by a person believing they are dead or non-existent?
explanation:
Cotard syndrome
Cotard syndrome is characterised by a person believing they are dead or non-existent. It tends to be related to depression.

Capgras syndrome
Capgras syndrome is characterised by a person believing their friend or relative had been replaced by an exact double.

Couvade syndrome
Couvade syndrome is also known as 'sympathetic pregnancy'. It affects fathers, particularly during the first and third trimesters of pregnancy, who suffer the somatic features of pregnancy.

De Clerambault's syndrome
De Clerambault's syndrome is characterised by a person believing that another individual (often a celebrity) is deeply in love with them. It typically affects females.

Othello syndrome
Othello syndrome is when the patient believes their partner is cheating on them. They may be threatening or stalk their partner. This seems to affect males more than females.

stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted with pneumonia. He drinks 20 units of alcohol per day. His liver function is normal. Approximately 12 hours into his admission he becomes unwell. His observations are shown below: Respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute Oxygen saturations 96% Blood pressure 123/76 mmHg Heart rate 106 bpm. Capillary blood glucose 4.1 mmol/L An ECG shows sinus tachycardia at a rate of 103 bpm. On examination, he appears tremulous and sweaty and complains of feeling anxious. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Chlordiazepoxide regimen and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
Regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
Stat dose of lorazepam and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide regimen and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
Chlordiazepoxide regimen and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement is correct. This patient is acutely withdrawing from alcohol. Symptoms usually begin 12 hours following reduction/cessation of alcohol intake. This patient will be undergoing assisted alcohol withdrawal in the inpatient setting, and as such will require prophylaxis of Wernicke's encephalopathy also.

250ml 10% glucose IV
250ml 10% glucose IV is incorrect, as the patient is not hypoglycaemic.

Regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
Regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement alone is incorrect, as the patient will require a benzodiazepine regimen for alcohol withdrawal also.

Stat dose of bisoprolol
Stat dose of bisoprolol is incorrect. The patient is in sinus tachycardia due to the alcohol withdrawal so bisoprolol will not treat the problem.

Stat dose of lorazepam and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement
Stat dose of lorazepam and regular high strength IM B vitamin replacement is incorrect. Lorazepam or oxazepam are sometimes used in alcohol withdrawal where there is evidence of alcoholic liver disease but this patient has documented normal LFTs. Also, a stat dose would not be sufficient to treat his alcohol withdrawal and he will require a weaning regimen.

stem: A 28-year-old man with known schizophrenia presents for his annual mental health review. His mental health has stabilised after the initiation of first-line treatment, however, his physical health seems to be deteriorating. You realise that his body mass index has increased over the past 5 years from 24kg/m² to 32kg/m² and at the same time, his cholesterol and triglyceride levels have almost doubled. What is the most likely responsible medication in this patient?
explanation:
Olanzapine
Olanzapine has a higher risk than other atypical antipsychotics for dyslipidaemia and obesity. Olanzapine has a higher risk than other atypical anti-psychotics for dyslipidaemia and is a first-line agent in the treatment of schizophrenia.

Aripiprazole
Aripiprazole is generally recognised as an atypical antipsychotic with a lower risk of causing dyslipidaemia.

Clozapine
Clozapine, one of the first atypical agents to be developed, does have a significant risk of dyslipidaemia. However, due to the significant risk of agranulocytosis, it is only used in patients resistant to other antipsychotic medication, not on the first presentation.

Quetiapine
Quetiapine has a lower risk of dyslipidaemia when compared with clozapine and olanzapine, however is seen to have a higher risk than aripiprazole and risperidone.

Risperidone
Risperidone is generally recognised as an atypical antipsychotic with a lower risk of causing dyslipidaemia.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has 3 days of dizziness, irritability, and diarrhoea after stopping a medication 5 days ago that she had been taking for several months. She was diagnosed with depression and prescribed an antidepressant, which she discontinued due to drowsiness as a side effect. Her vital signs are normal. She appears anxious but is otherwise well, with no signs of acute illness. Which drug was this patient most likely taking?
explanation:
Paroxetine
Paroxetine is correct. The most likely diagnosis is selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) discontinuation syndrome, which typically occurs within days of stopping the medication and includes symptoms such as dizziness, irritability, and diarrhoea, all of which are present in this patient. Paroxetine is the most likely cause due to its short half-life, which leads to a rapid drop in plasma levels and an increased risk of withdrawal effects. The onset of symptoms five days after abrupt discontinuation is consistent with paroxetine-induced discontinuation syndrome.

Escitalopram
Escitalopram is incorrect. While this is also an SSRI, it has a longer halflife than paroxetine, resulting in a slower decline in plasma concentration and milder withdrawal symptoms. This makes it less likely to cause the abrupt onset of dizziness, irritability, and diarrhoea observed in this patient. In addition, escitalopram is less sedating than paroxetine, making drowsiness a less likely reason for discontinuation in this case.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. Although this is also an SSRI, it has a very long half-life and active metabolites, leading to a gradual reduction in drug levels after discontinuation. This makes significant discontinuation symptoms such as dizziness, irritability, and diarrhoea less likely to occur within a few days of stopping the drug. Furthermore, fluoxetine is less sedating than paroxetine, making persistent drowsiness an unlikely cause for the patient to stop taking it.

Lofepramine
Lofepramine is incorrect because it is a tricyclic antidepressant and not typically used as a first-line treatment for depression. SSRIs such as paroxetine are preferred first-line due to their improved tolerability and safety profile. Withdrawal from lofepramine is also less likely to produce acute symptoms such as dizziness, irritability, and diarrhoea within a few days, as it has a longer half-life and lower risk of rapid-onset discontinuation syndrome.

Mirtazapine
Mirtazapine is incorrect as it is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant with a lower risk of discontinuation syndrome compared to SSRIs such as paroxetine. Although mirtazapine is strongly sedating and could cause drowsiness, leading to discontinuation, it is less likely to be used first-line. It is generally considered when SSRIs are not tolerated or fail to improve symptoms. Its withdrawal symptoms are usually mild and delayed, and dizziness and diarrhoea are much less common. Instead, mirtazapine withdrawal may cause insomnia and rebound anxiety.

stem: A 28-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is being commenced on clozapine in an outpatient clinic. He has previously had unsuccessful trials of olanzapine and risperidone. He is otherwise medically fit. When counselling him about common and potentially serious side effects, which of the following is most important to discuss and manage proactively from the outset? What is the most important side effect to counsel the patient about?
explanation:
Constipation
One of the most common side effects of clozapine is constipation/intestinal obstruction. Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility is an extremely common and potentially fatal side effect. It affects up to 60% of patients treated with clozapine due to its potent anticholinergic and antimuscarinic properties. This can range from simple constipation to life-threatening complications such as paralytic ileus, bowel obstruction, and faecal impaction, which carry a mortality rate of up to 20-30%. Due to the high incidence and severity, it is crucial to counsel patients about this risk before starting treatment and to initiate prophylactic laxatives (typically a stimulant and a softener) from day one. A 'no poo, no clozapine' policy is often adopted on inpatient wards, highlighting the clinical importance of monitoring bowel function closely throughout treatment.

Akathisia
Akathisia is a state of motor restlessness, which can be extremely distressing for patients. It is a well-recognised extrapyramidal side effect (EPSE) of antipsychotic medication. However, it is most commonly associated with first-generation (typical) antipsychotics and some second-generation agents like risperidone and aripiprazole. Clozapine has a very low affinity for dopamine D2 receptors, which is thought to mediate EPSEs. Consequently, it has a very low risk of causing akathisia and is sometimes used off-label to treat akathisia caused by other antipsychotics.

Diarrhoea
Diarrhoea is not a recognised side effect of clozapine. In fact, the opposite is true. Due to its significant anticholinergic effects on the gastrointestinal tract, clozapine slows gut transit time, leading to constipation. While any medication can cause idiosyncratic side effects, diarrhoea would be a very unusual reaction to clozapine. It is more commonly associated with other psychotropic medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or as a symptom of lithium toxicity.

Insomnia
Insomnia is not a typical side effect of clozapine. Clozapine is a potent antagonist at several receptors, including histamine H1 receptors, which results in significant sedation. This is a very common side effect, particularly during the initial titration phase, and is the reason clozapine is usually administered at night. While sleep architecture can be affected, frank insomnia is not a characteristic feature; hypersomnolence is far more common. Insomnia is more frequently reported with other medications like SSRIs or activating antipsychotics like aripiprazole.

Polyuria
Polyuria is not associated with clozapine. It is the classical hallmark of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, where the kidneys become resistant to the effects of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). This is a key side effect to monitor for in patients taking lithium for bipolar affective disorder. Clozapine does not have this effect on renal function. This option tests the ability to differentiate the side effect profiles of different major psychotropic medications.

stem: You are a junior doctor on the acute medical take. Your next patient has been admitted with an exacerbation of heart failure. Whilst exploring his past medical history he confides in you he was in a road traffic collision 3 months ago in which a family friend was killed. He explains he is struggling to sleep and feels he is constantly re-living the accident. He states he is afraid to leave the house in case it was to happen again and that any loud noises cause him to panic. He has increased his alcohol intake to try and forget about it and to help him sleep. Which of the following treatments is most likely to help this man?
options: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy
GP to review in one month
explanation:
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy
EMDR therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can be trialled in patients with severe cases of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Olanzapine
Olanzapine along with most other antipsychotics are not used in the management of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). NICE recommends a trial of risperidone in patients with severe cases of PTSD.

GP to review in one month
In mild cases lasting less than 4 weeks watchful waiting can be used. It may be appropriate in these scenarios for a GP to regularly review the patient. However, in the above case, given the man in the above scenario has experienced severe symptoms for the past 12 weeks, this option would not be appropriate.

Single-session debrief therapy
Single-session debrief therapy is not recommended following traumatic events and so this option is not correct.

Tricyclic antidepressant
Tricyclic antidepressants are not recommended in PTSD. If drug therapy is to be tried then SSRIs such as sertraline or venlafaxine (SNRI) can be tried.

stem: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance, after being found confused by members of the public for the fifth time in the past month. Upon review, he tells you that he came here by bicycle after spending the afternoon with his friends doing shopping, and then later tells you he spent today in the pub with his new dog. He smells strongly of alcohol and you notice a near-empty bottle of unlabelled spirit with him. On examination, he has an ataxic gait, dysdiadochokinesia and horizontal nystagmus. When you go back later to see him, he has forgotten your previous interaction. Which of the following explains his signs and symptoms?
explanation:
Korsakoff's syndrome
Korsakoff's syndrome is a complication of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It's features include: anterograde amnesia, retrograde amnesia, and confabulation. This man has presented to the emergency department with cerebellar signs, eye signs, amnesia, and is changing his story about recent events. He is also carrying around a tell-tale bottle of alcohol. However, this man also has features that make Korsakoff's syndrome the unifying diagnosis: anterograde amnesia (he forgets your interaction) and confabulation (he makes up two different stories about his day).

Cerebellar ataxia
Cerebellar ataxia, caused by alcohol use, haemorrhage, tumour, infection, or other cause, accounts for some of this man's symptoms, but it does not account for the specific symptoms that point to Korsakoff's disease.

Ethanol intoxication
Alcohol intoxication might produce unsteadiness and confusion or changing stories, but the specific neurological signs point away from this.

Methanol toxicity
Methanol toxicity is a possible cause of ataxia, poor coordination, and confusion. It may even contaminate unregulated alcohol products. However, it would likely also cause vomiting, abdominal pain, decreased consciousness, and can progress to respiratory failure.

Wernicke's encephalopathy
Wernicke's encephalopathy alone would account for most, though not all of his symptoms. The classic triad for this is ophthalmoplegia (often a lateral rectus palsy and/or horizontal nystagmus), confusion, and ataxia (though any cerebellar signs can be present).

stem: A 60-year-old male is admitted to the in-patient psychiatric unit last night. On reviewing him this morning, he is a poor historian, answering most questions minimally and stating he does not need to be here as he is deceased, and hospitals should be for living patients. What is the name of this delusional disorder and which condition is it most commonly associated with?
options: De Clerambault's syndrome and Major Depressive Disorder
Cotard syndrome and Major Depressive Disorder
Charles de Bonnet syndrome and Bipolar Disorder
explanation:
Cotard syndrome and Major Depressive Disorder
Cotard syndrome is associated with severe depression. This patient is presenting with Cotard's syndrome, a rare subtype of nihilistic delusions, in which they believe they or part of them is dead or does not exist. This is seen most commonly in severe depression, but is also associated with schizophrenia.

De Clerambault's syndrome and Major Depressive Disorder
De Clerambault's syndrome is not the correct delusional disorder for this patient's presentation.

Othello syndrome and Paranoid Schizophrenia
Othello syndrome is not the correct delusional disorder for this patient's presentation.

Capgras delusion and Dementia
Capgras delusion is not the correct delusional disorder for this patient's presentation.

Charles de Bonnet syndrome and Bipolar Disorder
Charles de Bonnet syndrome is not the correct delusional disorder for this patient's presentation.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of abdominal pain. She describes generalised abdominal discomfort that has been present constantly for the last four days. She has not experienced any changes to her bowel habit, and has no urinary symptoms. Her weight is stable. She is very concerned that these symptoms are due to an underlying ovarian cancer. She has presented to both primary and secondary care multiple times this year with similar symptoms. Each time, she has been convinced that she has ovarian cancer, and has not been reassured by a series of negative investigations, including blood tests and pelvic ultrasound scans. Her mother died of ovarian cancer in her sixties. Her blood test results are as follows: Hb 118 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 195 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 5.8 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 135 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 3.7 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 3.5 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 59 µmol/L (55 - 120) CA-125 31 U/mL (<46) What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
explanation:
Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis) is the persistent belief in the presence of an underlying serious disease, e.g. cancer. This patient has presented with an unshakeable conviction that she has a specific serious disease, i.e. ovarian cancer. Her conviction has not become any less strong in the face of negative investigations for the disease in question. This is characteristic of illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis), and has likely been contributed to by her mother dying of ovarian cancer.

Ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer can present insidiously, with vague symptoms such as abdominal pain. However, the diagnosis of ovarian cancer in this patient is made much less likely by a normal CA-125 level, and recent normal pelvic ultrasonography.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is also characterised by unexplained symptoms, with patients refusing to accept normal investigation findings as reassurance. However, in somatisation disorder, the symptoms are often more varied, and tend to be present for a longer period of time. The fixation on a specific diagnosis, rather than the symptoms per se, is more in keeping with hypochondriasis.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder is most typically associated with an unexplained loss of sensory or motor function.

Malingering
Malingering describes the fraudulent fabrication of symptoms with a calculated motive, such as financial gain or exemption from work duties. There is no suggestion that this patient has such a motive for seeking medical attention.

stem: As part of a home visit, a new mother undergoes an assessment of her mental health as she reports feeling miserable quite often in the week since giving birth. She reports feeling panicky for no clear reason at times, resulting in difficulty sleeping. She also reports feeling sad to the point of crying occasionally and has regular thoughts of worthlessness. After asking all questions, she has an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score of 9. The mother reports she is breastfeeding and has no significant past medical history. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Admission to hospital for further assessment
explanation:
Reassurance and support
The most appropriate treatment for this mother is reassurance and support. An Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) score of 9 is considered negative for depression, despite her reported symptoms. These symptoms likely indicate 'baby blues,' a common and temporary condition affecting many new mothers within the first two weeks postpartum. Baby blues typically involve mood swings, anxiety, sadness, and irritability but do not usually require medical treatment beyond emotional support and reassurance. Encouraging her to rest, seek support from loved ones, and communicate her feelings can help her navigate this transient phase.

Admission to hospital for further assessment
Admission to hospital for further assessment is incorrect in this case. Hospitalisation is typically considered for severe postpartum depression or puerperal psychosis, conditions that involve intense symptoms such as severe mood swings, confusion, hallucinations, or delusional thinking. The mother's EPDS score of 9 indicates a low likelihood of major depression.

Cognitive behavioural therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is incorrect in this case because it is primarily used for postnatal depression. The mother's EPDS score of 9 suggests she is not currently experiencing postnatal depression but rather the 'baby blues,' a common and temporary condition postpartum. CBT may be considered if her symptoms persist beyond the typical duration of baby blues (about two weeks) or if her condition worsens.

Continue breastfeeding and trial paroxetine
Continue breastfeeding and trial paroxetine is incorrect because the patient's symptoms align with 'baby blues,' a mild and temporary condition that typically resolves without medication. Although paroxetine is recommended by SIGN due to its low milk/plasma ratio, it is not necessary in this case as the patient’s condition does not require pharmacological treatment.

Discontinue breastfeeding and trial fluoxetine
Discontinue breastfeeding and trial fluoxetine is incorrect as antidepressants are reserved for significant postnatal depression, which the mother does not currently have, given her EPDS score of 9. Additionally, breastfeeding offers benefits for both mother and baby and therefore, if required, alternative medications to allow for the continuation of breastfeeding is generally preferred.

stem: Which one of the following is not a recognised feature of anorexia nervosa?
explanation:
Reduced growth hormone levels
In anorexia nervosa, growth hormone (GH) levels are typically elevated rather than reduced. This elevation occurs as a compensatory mechanism in response to the state of starvation and malnutrition. The body increases GH secretion to mobilise fat stores and maintain blood glucose levels during periods of nutritional deprivation. This represents a physiological adaptation to conserve energy and maintain essential metabolic functions during starvation. Despite elevated GH levels, patients with anorexia nervosa often have low insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels due to GH resistance in the liver, which is another adaptation to the malnourished state.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is a recognised feature of anorexia nervosa. It can occur due to multiple mechanisms including poor dietary intake, renal potassium wasting (particularly in patients who purge through vomiting or laxative abuse), and shifts in potassium distribution related to refeeding. Hypokalaemia can lead to serious cardiac complications including arrhythmias and is an important parameter to monitor in these patients.

Low LH
Low LH (luteinising hormone) is a common finding in anorexia nervosa. The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is suppressed in response to malnutrition and low body weight, resulting in reduced gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulsatility and consequently low LH levels. This contributes to the amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea frequently observed in female patients with anorexia nervosa.

Impaired glucose tolerance
Impaired glucose tolerance is indeed a recognised feature of anorexia nervosa. Patients often display abnormal glucose metabolism, including delayed insulin secretion and impaired glucose tolerance. This occurs as an adaptive response to starvation, with the body attempting to preserve glucose for essential functions, particularly brain metabolism.

Low FSH
Low FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) occurs in anorexia nervosa for the same reason as low LH - suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis due to malnutrition. The reduced FSH levels contribute to impaired follicular development in females and reduced spermatogenesis in males with anorexia nervosa, resulting in reproductive dysfunction.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with recurrent vomiting. Her mother reports she doesn't eat alongside her family, but she has found empty food packets hidden in her room. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bulimia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa is the correct answer. The combination of recurrent vomiting and secretive eating behaviour evidences this. Bulimia nervosa is characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviours, such as self-induced vomiting, to avoid weight gain. These episodes typically occur in secret due to feelings of shame or guilt.

Anorexia nervosa
Anorexia nervosa is incorrect. This diagnosis involves significant food restriction and intense fear of gaining weight. Food packets would not be expected to be found, as there is often an associated fear of food and complete avoidance, rather than secretive behaviours.

Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID)
Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) is incorrect. ARFID involves avoidance of food due to sensory characteristics, fear of choking, or a lack of interest in eating, without body image disturbance or fear of gaining weight. It does not involve binge eating or compensatory behaviours like vomiting. The girl in this scenario is consuming food in secret and vomiting, which are not features of ARFID. Therefore, this diagnosis does not fit the clinical picture.

Binge eating disorder
Binge eating disorder is incorrect. Recurrent episodes of binge eating characterise this diagnosis without compensatory behaviours such as vomiting, excessive exercise, or fasting. The presence of vomiting in this case excludes binge-eating disorder. Thus, the behaviours described are more consistent with bulimia nervosa.

Rumination disorder
Rumination disorder is incorrect. Rumination disorder involves the repeated regurgitation of food after eating, which may be re-chewed, reswallowed, or spit out. It is typically observed in infants or individuals with developmental disorders, though it can rarely occur in adolescents. However, it is not associated with binge eating or hidden food, nor is it a voluntary behaviour aimed at weight control. The scenario points to deliberate vomiting after binge eating, which rules out rumination disorder.

stem: A 93-year-old female patient on the ward is brought to your attention by the nurses. They are concerned she is experiencing visual hallucinations. She was admitted following a decline in mobility that was thought to be secondary to a urinary tract infection (UTI). She has improved clinically and biochemically during her time on the ward and she is awaiting a increase package of care before discharge. You review the patient who tells you she earlier saw very small children running across the end of the bed. She reports she regularly sees similar images at home and has done so for many years. She has a background of hypertension, depression and age-related macular degeneration. What is the most appropriate step in this patient's management?
options: Consider treatment failure of her UTI
explanation:
Reassure the patient
This most likely represents Charles Bonnet syndrome. Reassurance is usually the best treatment, helping people to understand and come to terms with their hallucinations.

Urgent psychiatric evaluation
It is importance to ensure there is not an alternative cause e.g. infection, psychosis, dementia (particularly Lewy body dementia), intoxication, metabolic abnormalities, focal neurological illness.

stem: A 44-year-old woman attends the clinic for review. She was started on sertraline 12 months ago for severe depression. She informs you that the symptoms of depression have now resolved. For how long should she continue with treatment?
explanation:
6 months
Antidepressants should be continued for at least 6 months after remission of symptoms to decrease the risk of relapse.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents to the emergency department with tremors and restlessness. He is visibly anxious and pacing up and down. He admits having last had 'a drink' 8 hours ago. He also describes having taken some morphine several hours prior, but cannot quantify this. On examination, he is anxious and sweating. Physical observations are normal except for a heart rate of 118 bpm. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. A general tremor is noted. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide
Alcohol withdrawal symptoms: 6-12 hours seizures: 36 hours delirium tremens: 72 hours. This patient is likely experiencing alcohol withdrawal. Initial symptoms, 6-12 hours after last consumption, include the features seen here - tremor, sweating, anxiety and tachycardia. Later features include seizures and delirium tremens. Patients presenting to hospital with features of alcohol withdrawal should be treated with long-acting benzodiazepines first-line, such as chlordiazepoxide or diazepam.

Lorazepam
Lorazepam is a short-acting benzodiazepine and not as preferable for this patient. It may be more suitable for patients with a history of hepatic impairment.

Methadone
Methadone is an opioid agonist used in the management of withdrawal from opioid addiction. Although patients experiencing opioid addiction may present with similar symptoms, they typically experience nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and rhinorrhoea, which are not seen here.

Naloxone
Naloxone is used in the management of opioid overdose. Rather than being agitated as in this scenario, the patient would be drowsy, have pinpoint pupils and potentially respiratory depression.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is an anticonvulsant. It is not typically recommended for alcohol withdrawal seizures as its effectiveness for these is questionable. It would not be appropriate here.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with dizziness, nausea, vivid dreams, irritability, and a sensation of electric shocks in her head. She had been treated for moderate depression for over a year and reported significant improvement. Two days ago, she abruptly stopped taking her antidepressant without medical advice. Her symptoms began within 48 hours of stopping the medication. She denies any recent illness, substance use, or changes in routine. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely antidepressant she was taking?
explanation:
Paroxetine
Paroxetine is correct because it is well known to have the highest incidence of discontinuation symptoms among antidepressants. These symptoms typically begin within 1–3 days of stopping the medication and may include dizziness, nausea, insomnia, irritability, vivid dreams, and paraesthesiae described as “electric shocks.” This patient’s presentation is classic, with symptom onset 48 hours after abrupt cessation. Paroxetine has a relatively short half-life and lacks an active metabolite, which contributes to the severity of withdrawal symptoms when stopped suddenly.

Citalopram
Citalopram is incorrect as it is associated with a lower risk of discontinuation symptoms compared to paroxetine. While it is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, its longer half-life and slower offset mean that abrupt cessation is less likely to produce sudden and severe symptoms. It may cause mild withdrawal effects, but these are typically less intense than the presentation described. As per the BNF, discontinuation symptoms are more common with paroxetine and less likely with drugs like fluoxetine and citalopram.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect because it is one of the least likely antidepressants to cause discontinuation symptoms. It has a long half-life and an active metabolite (norfluoxetine) that persists for days to weeks, which provides a natural tapering effect. For this reason, fluoxetine is sometimes used to help patients transition off other antidepressants with shorter half-lives.

Mirtazapine
Mirtazapine is incorrect because while it can cause withdrawal symptoms if stopped suddenly, they are typically mild and not characterised by vivid dreams or electric-shock sensations. Mirtazapine acts through noradrenergic and serotonergic pathways but lacks the potent serotonin reuptake inhibition of paroxetine, which is strongly linked to discontinuation effects.

Sertraline
Sertraline is incorrect because although it can cause discontinuation symptoms, these are generally less frequent and less severe than those seen with paroxetine. Sertraline has a longer half-life and a more gradual offset, which reduces the likelihood of abrupt withdrawal effects. When symptoms do occur, they tend to be milder and shorter-lived. The vivid sensory disturbances and rapid onset of symptoms described in this case are more characteristic of paroxetine discontinuation.

stem: A 34-year-old man originally from West Africa is seen in January with depression. There is no past medical history of note but he is known to smoke cannabis. He has had similar episodes for the past two winters. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Seasonal affective disorder
The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Seasonal affective disorder. This condition is characterised by recurrent episodes of depression that usually occur during the same season each year, in this case, winter. The fact that the patient has had similar episodes for the past two winters strengthens this diagnosis.
